title: The Next School of War: Educating for Tomorrow’s Battlefield
gist: Marine Corps University's president and a senior faculty member describe reforms pushing professional military education toward a classified, all-domain curriculum with battle labs, wargaming, and AI integration to prepare officers for multidomain warfare against China and Russia, arguing military education has lagged the changing character of war.

themes.theme: The case that military education has fallen behind the changing character of war

insights.claim: Most major militaries now see war as inherently multidomain and defined by converging effects that combine cyber, space, and the electromagnetic spectrum with land, sea, and air maneuvers, extending operational art to coordinating what the authors call a 'symphony of capabilities.'
insights.speaker: Brig. Gen. Matthew Tracy and Benjamin Jensen
insights.so_what: Signals a structural, cross-service shift in doctrine toward multidomain integration (cyber, space, EW) that should inform how defense-tech and C2/battle-management software vendors pitch to the Pentagon.
insights.quote: Operational art extends to coordinating a \u201csymphony of capabilities.\u201d
insights.locator: Most major militaries now see war as inherently multidomain

insights.claim: Professional military education tends to reinforce stale seminars and lectures disconnected from the technical reality of modern warfare, with students spending more time on classical texts like The History of the Peloponnesian War than reviewing modern war plans.
insights.speaker: Brig. Gen. Matthew Tracy and Benjamin Jensen
insights.so_what: A direct critique from a war college president signals institutional appetite for curriculum-driven defense-tech and simulation/training vendor contracts.
insights.quote: Students spend more time reading The History of the Peloponnesian War and admiring ground campaigns from the U.S. Civil War than they do reviewing modern war plans.
insights.locator: Yet, military education has not kept up

insights.claim: The fact that after months of bombing and intermittent clashes, Iran retains the ability to launch drone, missile, and cyber attacks should be a clarion call about the difficulty of breaking modern anti-access and area-denial networks, with China presenting an order-of-magnitude larger version of the same challenge via deeper space, cyber, and long-strike capabilities.
insights.speaker: Brig. Gen. Matthew Tracy and Benjamin Jensen
insights.so_what: Explicitly frames China as an order-of-magnitude harder A2/AD problem than Iran or Russia-Ukraine, reinforcing continued high-priority Pentagon investment in counter-A2/AD, long-range strike, and space/cyber capabilities.
insights.quote: The fact that after months of bombing and intermittent clashes, Iran retains the ability to launch drone, missile, and cyber attacks, should be a clarion call.
insights.locator: This technical requirement is driven by the challenge

themes.theme: Marine Corps University's classified curriculum reforms

insights.claim: Marine Corps University built a pilot curriculum for Joint All-Domain Operations at the top-secret/sensitive compartmented information level, centered on the Command and Staff College under faculty leads Nathan Packard and Joseph McAlarnen, reorienting a curriculum that had only moderately changed over the prior 10 years.
insights.speaker: Brig. Gen. Matthew Tracy and Benjamin Jensen
insights.so_what: A concrete, named case study of a U.S. war college shifting core curriculum into classified, all-domain territory — a template other services may replicate, relevant to firms selling classified simulation/wargaming platforms.
insights.locator: We started by building a pilot curriculum

insights.claim: By graduation from Intermediate Level School, a major must be able to coordinate distinct advantages across enough domains to execute maneuver, fires, and logistics pulses and to fight a single Joint Task Force at the echelon II level, while Top Level School graduates (lieutenant colonels) must be able to coordinate multiple Joint Task Forces to achieve theater objectives, including grounding in nuclear effects and delivery systems.
insights.speaker: Brig. Gen. Matthew Tracy and Benjamin Jensen
insights.so_what: Defines concrete new graduation competency standards (echelon II JTF command for majors, multi-JTF theater coordination for lieutenant colonels) that mark a measurable escalation in officer readiness expectations.
insights.locator: By graduation from Intermediate Level School

insights.claim: Expecting officers to master modern warfare using exclusively unclassified materials resembles teaching surgery to medical students restricted from cutting on cadavers, according to the authors, who argue large segments of military education must occur in secure spaces where students can grapple with actual capabilities and real-world adversary threats.
insights.speaker: Brig. Gen. Matthew Tracy and Benjamin Jensen
insights.so_what: Explains the rationale driving expanded SCIF/classified-facility investment at military education institutions, a durable demand driver for secure-facility construction and classified IT infrastructure.
insights.quote: expecting officers to master modern warfare using exclusively unclassified materials resembles teaching surgery to medical students restricted from cutting on cadavers
insights.locator: As a result, expecting officers to master modern warfare

insights.claim: Faculty development now sends historians to space camp to understand orbital mechanics and political scientists to study command and control and joint fires, with instructors required to pair academic writing with attendance at operational courses, such as a historian writing on the Overland Campaign also attending the Combined Forces Land Component Commander course.
insights.speaker: Brig. Gen. Matthew Tracy and Benjamin Jensen
insights.so_what: Illustrates an operational-realism requirement being imposed on academic faculty, a model that signals rising demand for joint-certifying course capacity and operational-fluency training programs.
insights.quote: Our historians now attend space camp to understand orbital mechanics.
insights.locator: Transforming the curriculum also required a new approach

insights.claim: Students in the pilot classified curriculum were able to support Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency wargames and real-world fleet problems, and participated in evaluating joint warfare education, including writing a commander's estimate in a time-compressed, high-uncertainty setting.
insights.speaker: Brig. Gen. Matthew Tracy and Benjamin Jensen
insights.so_what: Early evidence the reformed curriculum is already feeding directly into DARPA wargaming and fleet problem-solving, a tangible link between military education output and operational/procurement decision-making.

insights.claim: The majority of students learn at distance education locations at major bases, and because SCIFs are already present there alongside students, Marine Corps Distance Education and Training has introduced a blended seminar program teaching all-domain war at the classified level, extending classified education beyond the main campus.
insights.speaker: Brig. Gen. Matthew Tracy and Benjamin Jensen
insights.so_what: Signals scaling of classified military education infrastructure (SCIF-enabled distance learning) beyond a single flagship campus, a broader base for secure-facility and classified-content vendors.

themes.theme: Battle labs, wargaming, and AI integration

insights.claim: The university's Gray Scholars program at the Command and Staff College had students support real-world efforts on urban warfare and DARPA's mosaic warfare concept, and this battle-lab model has since evolved at the School of Advanced Warfighting, where students worked with the Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Office to explore how AI can augment military planning.
insights.speaker: Brig. Gen. Matthew Tracy and Benjamin Jensen
entities: Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Office
insights.so_what: Names a specific channel (CDAO collaboration with School of Advanced Warfighting) through which AI planning-augmentation concepts are being tested inside professional military education, relevant to AI/defense-tech vendors targeting DoD planning tools.
insights.locator: Much of it started with the Gray Scholars program

insights.claim: Since the Brute Krulak Center's formation in 2016, the university has run an annual wargaming competition called Sea Dragon (starting 2018) that has evolved to integrate joint effects and even non-strategic nuclear weapons, and has been replicated by the international Fight Club Society and the former Training and Education Command Warfighting Society.
insights.speaker: Brig. Gen. Matthew Tracy and Benjamin Jensen
insights.so_what: Documents an eight-year track record of institutionalized wargaming (Sea Dragon) that now spans classified and unclassified formats and non-strategic nuclear scenarios, relevant to wargaming/simulation software providers.
insights.locator: Since the formation of the Brute Krulak Center in 2016

insights.claim: AI integration at Marine Corps University dates to 2018's Project Athena, which used wargame tournaments to generate human data convertible into machine courses of action, continuing through a DARPA collaboration on STORM models testing whether genetic algorithms could help develop course-of-action advisers, and evolving further as large language models altered how the field thought about AI.
insights.speaker: Brig. Gen. Matthew Tracy and Benjamin Jensen
insights.so_what: An eight-year AI-in-military-planning R&D lineage (Project Athena to STORM to LLM-era tools) that gives a concrete history for evaluating maturity of Pentagon-adjacent AI course-of-action advisory technology.
insights.locator: It started in 2018 with Project Athena

insights.claim: The authors argue AI is a general-purpose technology that must be adapted to the fog and friction inherent in warfare, and that the university will create classroom environments where students learn how models work and what problems they can and cannot solve in modern campaigns, cautioning that 'stochastic parroting is not a method.'
insights.speaker: Brig. Gen. Matthew Tracy and Benjamin Jensen
insights.so_what: A skeptical, capability-bounded framing of military AI adoption from a war-college leadership team — useful signal that Pentagon education institutions are pushing back against uncritical AI hype even as adoption expands.
insights.quote: Just like hope, stochastic parroting is not a method.
insights.locator: The fact is, AI is a general-purpose technology

themes.theme: What the reforms preserve from traditional education

insights.claim: The authors argue certain foundational elements endure regardless of AI and classified curriculum reforms: tactics and military theory, civil-military relations and the profession of arms including officers' ethical obligations under the constitutional framework, and military history, strategy, and international relations to inoculate officers against the hubris of the present.
insights.speaker: Brig. Gen. Matthew Tracy and Benjamin Jensen
insights.so_what: Clarifies the reform is additive rather than a wholesale replacement of classical military education — relevant context for assessing how radically PME institutions are actually changing versus rebalancing.
insights.locator: Amidst the introduction of classified curriculums

insights.claim: The authors conclude that sustaining and expanding these reforms will require robust institutional support, including funds for expanding classified infrastructure and building custom analytical tools, plus expanded training so civilian academic faculty can work alongside seasoned warfighters rather than being displaced.
insights.speaker: Brig. Gen. Matthew Tracy and Benjamin Jensen
insights.so_what: Signals a forthcoming budget ask for classified infrastructure and custom analytical tooling at military education institutions — a funding line to watch in defense education/training budgets.
insights.locator: To sustain and expand this evolution
